b: Parasites are organisms that live in or on a human host and cause harm. They include protozoa (single-celled) and helminths (worms).
Malaria — extra detail because it is important:

Malaria is transmitted by the bite of a female Anopheles mosquito. The Plasmodium parasite enters the red blood cells and destroys them, causing the characteristic fever. There are four main species: - Plasmodium falciparum — most dangerous
Prevention of malaria: - Insecticide-treated bed nets - Indoor residual spraying - Prophylactic drugs for travellers (Doxycycline, Atovaquone-Proguanil)

qs.q: An adult patient presenting with chronic microcytic hypochromic anemia in a developing country is evaluated for gastrointestinal blood loss. Laboratory investigations reveal occult blood in the stool caused by a parasitic infection that represents a leading global cause of iron deficiency anemia. Which parasite is responsible?
qs.e: Hookworms attach to the intestinal mucosa and cause chronic blood loss, making them the leading cause of iron deficiency anemia in the developing world. Giardia primarily causes fat and carbohydrate malabsorption by decreasing lactase rather than chronic occult blood loss.

qs.q: Which parasitic infection is treated using praziquantel, a drug that increases calcium ion permeability to cause spastic paralysis of the worm?
qs.e: Praziquantel increases calcium permeability leading to spastic paralysis and detachment, making it a primary treatment for schistosomiasis. Strongyloidiasis is typically treated with ivermectin instead.

qs.q: An individual who consumed undercooked freshwater fish develops a parasitic infection of the biliary system. How does the parasite infect the human host?
o: Consumption of raw aquatic plants carrying rediae stages
Ingestion of unhatched eggs present in contaminated mud
Direct skin penetration by free-swimming cercariae
Ingestion of metacercariae encysted in fish muscle
qs.e: Clonorchis sinensis cercariae penetrate freshwater fish to become metacercariae, which humans ingest by eating undercooked fish. Free-swimming cercaria penetration is characteristic of Schistosoma.

qs.q: A 42-year-old man who recently traveled to South America presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and a solitary liver lesion. What is the most common extraintestinal manifestation of this systemic parasitic infection?
qs.e: Hepatic amoebiasis is recognized as the most common extraintestinal manifestation of amoebiasis. Brain and splenic abscesses are much rarer complications of the infection.

qs.q: During a gynecological examination, a clinician observes characteristic physical signs of a urogenital parasitic infection in a female patient. Which set of findings is classically associated with female trichomoniasis?
o: Painful vesicular lesions, clear exudate, and inguinal lymphadenopathy
Pruritic vaginitis, greenish-yellow discharge, and strawberry mucosa
Hyperkeratotic plaques, thick white curd-like discharge, and normal pH
Profuse watery gray discharge with a strong fishy odor upon whiff test
qs.e: Classic clinical features in females include pruritic vaginitis, a greenish-yellow discharge, strawberry mucosa, and dysuria. Vesicles indicate herpes simplex, white curd-like discharge indicates candidiasis, and a fishy odor indicates bacterial vaginosis.

qs.q: Which specific white blood cell type is primarily responsible for mounting an immune response against parasitic infections and helminths through the release of major basic protein?
o: C. Basophils for allergic reactions and histamine release
A. Neutrophils for bacterial and fungal defense
D. Monocytes for phagocytosis and antigen presentation
B. Eosinophils for parasitic defense via major basic protein
qs.e: Eosinophils play a primary role in defending against parasitic infections by releasing major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein. Neutrophils, on the other hand, specialize in bacterial and fungal phagocytosis as first responders.

qs.q: An 18-month-old infant is brought to the pediatric clinic with fever, generalized lymphadenopathy, and unilateral periorbital edema after living in an endemic rural mud-brick dwelling. Which demographic group is most frequently diagnosed with symptomatic acute manifestations of this parasitic infection?
qs.e: Acute Chagas disease presents with prominent systemic symptoms most frequently in young children under 2 years of age. Older individuals typically present decades later with chronic cardiac or gastrointestinal manifestations.

qs.q: Which parasitic infection is commonly linked to the ingestion of contaminated raspberries from Central America?
qs.e: Cyclospora cayetanensis infection is typically associated with eating raspberries from Central America, water, or unpasteurized apple cider. Other parasites like Giardia have different primary sources such as diapered infants and water supplies.

ai.title: Parasitic Infections
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Parasitic infections are common in East Africa, presenting with fever, anaemia, diarrhoea or eosinophilia. Clinical reasoning hinges on history, simple tests and empirical treatment when investigations are limited.

sections.p: Parasites are organisms that live in or on humans, causing disease through mechanical damage, toxin release or immune activation. In low‑resource settings, malaria, schistosomiasis, soil‑transmitted helminths and protozoal diarrhoea dominate.
Protozoa are single‑cell, often motile; helminths are multicellular worms with specialised tissues. Life cycles involve intermediate hosts or environmental stages.
b: Plasmodium: erythrocytic schizogony; Schistosoma: cercariae penetrate skin; Ascaris: eggs passed in stool, hatch in gut

t.b: Identify parasite morphology in blood, stool or tissue; confirms species and guides treatment

sections.p: Transmission routes vary: mosquito bite for malaria, skin contact with contaminated water for schistosomiasis, ingestion of contaminated food or soil for helminths, and faecal–oral for protozoa.
b: Malaria: Anopheles mosquito → blood stage → liver stage → relapse

t.b: Detects Plasmodium antigens; positive = treat with artemisinin‑based combination

sections.p: Clinical spectrum ranges from asymptomatic carriage to severe anaemia, organ failure or death. Key presentations: fever with chills, anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly, diarrhoea, eosinophilia.
b: Malaria: fever, rigors, anaemia, cerebral complications

t.b: Anaemia, thrombocytopenia, eosinophilia; helps gauge severity

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, rely on history, simple microscopy, RDTs and basic labs. When unavailable, empirical treatment guided by epidemiology is acceptable.
b: Microscopy of blood smear for malaria

t.b: Detects parasites; confirms species and parasitaemia level; high parasitaemia = severe disease
Identify ova of Ascaris, hookworm, Trichuris; presence indicates infection
Positive indicates exposure; not always available

sections.p: Treat the causative organism, provide supportive care and address complications. Prevention focuses on vector control, sanitation and mass drug administration.

t.b: First‑line for Plasmodium falciparum; effective, low resistance in East Africa
Single dose for schistosomiasis; safe in pregnancy
Treats Ascaris, hookworm, Trichuris; safe in pregnancy

sections.p: Remember that severe malaria presents with high parasitaemia (>5%) and may need parenteral artesunate. Schistosomiasis can cause portal hypertension; look for splenomegaly and ascites. Soil‑transmitted helminths often present with anaemia and eosinophilia.
b: If RDT negative but clinical suspicion high, repeat smear or treat empirically

t.b: Rule out pulmonary helminths (e.g., Strongyloides) in immunocompromised

whenToSeekHelp: Severe anaemia (Hb <7 g/dL), altered sensorium, persistent vomiting, jaundice, haemoglobinuria, shock

faq.q: Why is malaria still a problem in East Africa?
faq.a: High vector density, limited bed‑net coverage and emerging drug resistance keep malaria endemic.

faq.q: How do you differentiate malaria from typhoid fever?
faq.a: Malaria shows parasitaemia on smear/RDT; typhoid has Widal titre, but both can present with fever and abdominal pain.

faq.q: What is the first step if a patient has eosinophilia and chronic diarrhoea?
faq.a: Consider helminthic infection; start albendazole and investigate stool ova/cysts.
